en: The Questions of King Milinda:
The Chapter on Similes,
Section on the Earth.
5. The Question on the Mountain’s Five Qualities “Venerable Nāgasena, when you say that ‘five qualities of a mountain should be adopted,’ which are those five qualities that should be adopted?
“Just as a mountain, O Great King, is immovable, unshakable, and unwavering;”
In the same way, great king, a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, should not be excited by things that cause excitement, nor provoked by things that cause provocation;

he should not be deluded by things that cause delusion. Whether in honor or dishonor, in respect or disrespect, in esteem or lack of esteem, in fame or infamy, in blame or praise, in pleasure or pain, or in any desirable or undesirable phenomena—whether forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects—he should not be excited by those things that cause excitement, nor provoked by those things that cause provocation, nor deluded by those things that cause delusion.
One should not tremble, one should not waver; one should be as immovable as a mountain.
This, O Great King, is the first quality of a mountain that should be adopted.
And this, O Great King, was spoken by the Blessed One, the God above Gods:
"Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the wind,
so too [the wise] remain unmoved amidst blame and praise."
"The wise do not contract [themselves]," it is said.

Furthermore, Great King, just as a mountain is firm and not associated with anything, even so, Great King, a practitioner of yoga must be firm and unassociated; he should not form any association with anyone.
This, great king, is the second quality of a mountain that should be adopted.
And this was said, great king, by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods:
“Unmixed with householders...”
“Both of these by those who live homeless;
one who wanders without a home and has few desires— him I call a brahmin.”
Furthermore, Great King, a seed does not grow on a mountain;
even so, Great King, a practitioner of yoga should not allow defilements to grow within his own mind.
This, Great King, is the third quality of a mountain that should be adopted.
This was also said, Great King, by the Elder Subhūti:
“When a mind associated with lust arises in me;”
I myself shall examine it;
with one-pointed mind, I shall tame it.
Even when there is that which causes passion, do not be impassioned.
You feel aversion toward what is loathsome,
yet you are deluded by what is alluring;
therefore, depart from this forest.
This is the dwelling place of those who are purified,
stainless, and ascetic;
do not defile that which is pure.
"Depart quickly from the forest!
Furthermore, Great King, just as a mountain rises high aloft,
even so, Great King, must the practitioner of yoga be one whose knowledge has risen high aloft.
This, Great King, is the fourth quality of a mountain that should be adopted.
And this was said, Great King, by the Blessed One, the God above Gods:
“Laziness [should be overcome] by diligence...”
When the wise person,
having ascended the palace of wisdom,
drives away sorrow from the sorrowing multitude, they are free from grief.
‘As one standing on a mountain looks down upon those on the ground,
so does the wise man look down upon fools.
Furthermore, great king, a mountain is neither raised up nor lowered.
In the same way, great king, a yogi practicing yoga should not engage in rising or falling.
This, great king, is the fifth quality of a mountain that should be adopted.
And this was said, great king, by the female lay follower Cūḷasubhaddā while she was praising her own ascetics:
“The world is uplifted by gain and depressed by loss;
it is the same in both gain and loss.”
“Such are the ascetics for me.
This is the fifth question, on Mount Aṅga.
